text:
Krichene and Rendle’s [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) (KDD 2020) shows that sampled ranking metrics can reverse recommender comparisons relative to full-catalog metrics—even in expectation. Their [IJCAI extended abstract](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651) explicitly examines 99 sampled negatives. Thus, this benchmark’s HR@10 measures ranking within its sampled candidate sets; improvements do not establish improved full-catalog HR@10. Keep the pinned evaluator and qualify conclusions accordingly.

For fixed users and candidates, compare paired binary hits: let b count users hit only by the new model, c users hit only by baseline. Per-category ΔHR@10=(b−c)/200; macro improvement is the mean of four category differences. One net additional hit in one category changes macro HR@10 by 0.00125 (0.125 percentage points). Report b and c, since identical net gains can conceal very different disagreement counts. For a prespecified comparison, exact McNemar testing uses b conditional on b+c under Binomial(b+c, 0.5), assuming independent user pairs; see [Dietterich (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1162/089976698300017197). Such inference conditions on the fitted models and candidate protocol; it does not measure training-seed variability.

Repeated checkpoint and hyperparameter selection makes the winning validation gain optimistic. [Cawley and Talbot (2010)](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) documents overfitting the selection criterion and resulting evaluation bias. Ordinary post-selection McNemar p-values or paired bootstrap intervals do not account for that search. Treat small gains as exploratory, report search extent and paired counts, and reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched final evaluation after freezing selection.
